name: ArborX
workload: Spatial tree construction and nearest-neighbor search over growing numbers of objects, ArborX BVH versus Boost.Geometry.Index R-trees (several balancing algorithms) and nanoflann, as described for the ACM TOMS 2020 paper.
claimed_speedup: No numeric ratio confirmed. Paper text seen only as a search-result summary: tree construction is similar for ArborX and Boost.Geometry.Index (nanoflann loses competitiveness at large object counts); nearest-neighbor search is significantly faster in ArborX than in both Boost.Geometry.Index and nanoflann for larger object counts, especially the 'hollow' point distribution.
stars_or_usage: 242 stars; Trilinos/Kokkos ecosystem library; ACM TOMS papers (2020 and 2025 v2.0)
tradeoffs: Kokkos-based performance-portable C++ library (CPU threads plus CUDA/HIP/SYCL GPU backends) with optional distributed trees; the BVH is built for static or batch-rebuilt data rather than being a dynamic insert/delete R-tree; heavier build dependency than a header-only R-tree.
caveats: The paper (ACM TOMS 2020, doi 10.1145/3412558, arXiv 1908.11807) and its numbers could not be opened in this session: arxiv.org, ar5iv, dl.acm.org, osti.gov and dalg24.github.io were blocked by the cloud egress proxy, so the claim wording comes from a WebSearch summary of the paper, not from reading it. Hardware, compiler, flags, Boost and nanoflann versions are unknown. I opened the repo page, CITATION.bib (lists the 2020 TOMS paper and a 2025 'ArborX Library: Version 2.0' TOMS paper, doi 10.1145/3772288) and benchmarks/bvh_driver (bvh_driver.cpp present) but found no README numbers; whether the Boost/nanoflann comparison code is in the repo is unconfirmed. A verifier with paper access should fill numbers and likely upgrade or confirm tier B.
found_via: WebSearch: '"faster than Boost.Geometry" C++ polygon OR "point in polygon" OR "spatial index" OR "intersection" library benchmark' (surfaced arXiv 1908.11807), then WebSearch 'ArborX performance portable geometric search library Boost.Geometry.Index nanoflann outperforms speedup results'; repo page github.com/arborx/ArborX

name: Pkd-tree (parallel kd-tree with batch updates)
baseline: CGAL kd-tree (Spatial_searching) and Boost.Geometry R-tree (also BHL-tree and Log-tree)
workload: Parallel kd-tree construction, batch insertion and deletion, k-nearest-neighbor, range query and range count on large point sets, compared with CGAL, Boost's sequential R-tree and other parallel kd-tree baselines (SIGMOD 2025 paper).
claimed_speedup: Paper text seen only as a search-result summary: 'orders of magnitude faster' than CGAL and BHL-tree on batch updates because those rebuild the whole tree after every update; 17.4-40.7x faster insertions and 3.27-21.7x faster deletions than the fastest baseline (Log-tree); 59.3x self-relative speedup for batch insertion and 52.4x for deletion on 96 cores; also compared against Boost's sequential R-tree for construction, kNN and range report (ratios not seen).
tradeoffs: Built on ParlayLib (git submodule) for shared-memory parallelism, so wins need many cores; low-dimensional point sets (kNN, range, count queries), not general geometry or polygons. The repo README says Pkd-tree is now integrated into PSI-Lib (github.com/ucrparlay/SpaceTreeLib, MIT, PPoPP 2026 'Parallel Dynamic Spatial Indexes') which adds orth-trees and space-filling-curve indexes.
caveats: The SIGMOD 2025 paper (doi 10.1145/3709712, arXiv 2411.09275) could not be opened in this session (arxiv.org, dl.acm.org, cs.ucr.edu and mirrors blocked), so every number comes from a WebSearch summary of the paper and was not checked against the page. The headline wins over CGAL are for batch updates where CGAL rebuilds the tree, not for static construction or single queries; the largest ratios are against Log-tree, which is not a named incumbent. The opened repo README confirms that a CGAL baseline can be built with -DCGAL=ON (a 'cgal' binary takes the same arguments) and a ParGeo branch exists, but gives no numbers, compiler, flags or CPU.
found_via: WebSearch: '"Parallel kd-tree with Batch Updates" Men Shen Gu Sun Pkd-tree compared CGAL Boost R-tree speedup'; repo page github.com/ucrparlay/Pkd-tree; lead from github.com/topics (SpaceTreeLib, spatial-index C++ topic page)

name: small_gicp
baseline: PCL pcl::VoxelGrid (voxel downsampling) and pcl::GICP / fast_gicp::GICP (registration)
workload: Voxel-grid downsampling of KITTI 00 LiDAR scans, and GICP odometry over KITTI 00, compared with PCL and fast_gicp; also kd-tree construction compared across its own single- and multi-threaded variants (all nanoflann-based).
claimed_speedup: Single-threaded small_gicp::voxelgrid_sampling about 1.3x faster than pcl::VoxelGrid; multi-threaded voxelgrid_sampling_tbb (6 threads) about 3.2x faster than pcl::VoxelGrid; single-thread small_gicp::GICP about 2.4x and 1.9x faster than pcl::GICP and fast_gicp::GICP; multi-threaded kd-tree construction up to 4x faster than its own single-thread version (README says 6x), and the single-thread kd-tree is about equal to nanoflann.
hardware: Not stated for the downsampling or GICP benchmarks (AMD 5995WX is mentioned only in a struck-through kd-tree note)
stars_or_usage: 1.0k stars; vcpkg port small-gicp; JOSS 2024 paper (doi 10.21105/joss.06948)
tradeoffs: Depends on Eigen; optional TBB or OpenMP; bundles nanoflann and Sophus; Python bindings. Aimed at LiDAR point-cloud registration and downsampling, not general geometry. The README warns against -march=native unless every linked library uses it (about 1.1x gain).
caveats: Baselines are PCL and fast_gicp, not Boost.Geometry, CGAL or GEOS, so it fits the geometry-spatial category only loosely (point-cloud spatial operations). Its kd-tree is nanoflann-derived and no faster than nanoflann single-threaded. README and BENCHMARK.md disagree on the multi-thread kd-tree gain (6x versus 4x). Benchmark scripts are public but CPU, compiler and flags are not stated for the PCL comparisons and only KITTI 00 was used. The JOSS paper was not opened.
found_via: vcpkg versions/baseline.json plus ports/small-gicp/vcpkg.json (port small-gicp); WebSearch 'kd-tree C++ library "faster than nanoflann" benchmark point cloud nearest neighbor'; github.com/koide3/small_gicp README and BENCHMARK.md

name: Arctern
workload: Vectorised GeoSeries operations (within, contains, intersects, intersection, area, distance, simplify, convex_hull, is_valid, is_simple and others) on a geometry dataset, comparing GeoPandas with Arctern single-thread and multi-thread (v0.2.0).
claimed_speedup: README: 'In the latest version 0.2.0, Arctern achieves 24x speedup against GeoPandas. Even under single-thread execution, Arctern outperforms GeoPandas 7x on average.' Also up to 36x for GPU-accelerated spatial-relation operations over CPU counterparts. The README bar chart (read by eye, per-operation) shows multi-thread bars from about 2x (geom_equals) to about 60x (is_simple) and a single-thread bar for geom_equals below GeoPandas.
tradeoffs: C++ core in cpp/ plus Python, Spark and GUI parts; conda-based build; the GPU path needs CUDA; the repo has seen no commits since June 2020 and the roadmap items (distributed GeoSeries, KNN) were never finished in this repo.
caveats: The baseline is GeoPandas, a Python wrapper over GEOS, so much of the gain is probably multi-threading and removing per-geometry Python overhead rather than a faster geometry algorithm; I did not verify what geometry engine Arctern's C++ core uses. Dataset, hardware, compiler and flags are not stated, and per-operation numbers exist only in an image. No comparison with GEOS called directly from C++. Dormant since 2020.
found_via: github.com/topics/geospatial?l=c%2B%2B (topic listing), then the repo README; search aimed at GEOS-faster-than claims
